abstract.p: This brief elegy praises Sir Walter Waller’s valour, physical excellence, and learning through comparisons with classical gods, suggesting his excellence rivals Mars, Adonis, and Minerva. It then shifts to lament, presenting his death as a loss not just to individuals but to England as a whole. The poem ends by contrasting the burial of his body with the salvation of his soul, now honoured in heaven.

lg.l: I’de praise thy valour, but Mars ginn’s to frowne
And feares when Sol’s alofte that Mars must downe
I’de praise thy forme, but Venus cries amaine
Sir Walter Waller will my Adonies Adonis staine.
I’de praise thy learning but Minerva cries,
Then Athens fame must creepe when Waller’s dies flies
Asist us England in our dolefull Song.
When such limmes fade, thy flourish last’s not long
Earth hath his earth which doth his corpes inroll,
Angells tune Requiems to his blessed soule.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Sir Walter Waller (b. 1544 – d. 7 July 1599) was a Sussex landowner and soldier, knighted in 1572. He served as a captain in the English forces in the Netherlands in the 1580s, including at Rheinberg and Ostend, and was present during a garrison revolt at Ostend in 1588. He died intestate and was buried at Speldhurst in Kent. His wife, Anne Choute, died in September 1624.

div.head: Notes
div.p: In both copies, the poem is transmitted alongside a companion poem on Anne Choute , together forming a paired husband and wife set ().
